newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan exporters seen dragging dollar down vs yen.
newsitem.headline: Japan exporters seen dragging dollar down vs yen.

text.p: The dollar is likely to be dragged down against the yen until the end of March as Japanese firms repatriate funds for their book closings, but dealers said this does not necessarily signal an end to its bull run.

"Demand for yen has been rising ahead of institutions' book closings and on their judgement that the dollar had gone far enough to cash in profits," said Shuji Ayabe, deputy general manager of the foreign exchange department at Fuji Bank Ltd.

This was a shift for Japanese exporters, who had until only recently refrained from converting their overseas earnings and assets into yen, based on the dominant view that the dollar would keep rising.
But since Tuesday, they have sold dollars on the growing perception that a further advance by the dollar was difficult.
Some Japanese exporters are also hedging risks against an unexpected rise in the yen beyond the March period by arranging for dollar sales through forward contracts and options.
The dollar was standing at 121 yen in mid-afternoon Tokyo trade on Wednesday after rising close to 125 yen in early February.

The latest wave of Japanese dollar sales was also sparked by news on Monday that Mitsubishi Heavy Industries plans to liquidate all its dollar-denominated deposits worth about $700 million and convert them into yen.

"Similar actions, more or less, by other Japanese companies will follow, given the dollar's rise of nearly 10 yen since the start of this year and its powerful recovery from around 80 yen (in 1995)," said Fuji Bank's Ayabe.

Noriyuki Takano, assistant director of forex sales at Barclays Bank Plc, said: "There is potential for the dollar to fall to 118 yen by the end of March, and for a return to 125 yen to become almost impossible".
On the other hand, exporters said they were in no rush to dump dollars in large amounts, since fundamental factors still favour the greenback.

"We would like to sell dollars steadily on the rises, but not urgently," said Tomoo Suzuki, manager of the Treasury division at NEC Corp. "Given the small chance of a quick rise in Japanese interest rates, stable inflow of funds into yen assets is unlikely," he added.
An official at the finance department of a Japanese car maker also added, "The dollar is basically in a 120-125 yen range and I don't expect any fast freefall of the dollar."
Fuji Bank's Ayabe said it will take time to see whether the current dollar's fall will end up as merely a seasonal move.

But if the adverse effects on the economy from a consumption tax hike in April are less than economists anticipate and the Bank of Japan's quarterly corporate survey that month shows better-than-expected business sentiment, the yen could power higher, he added.
Demand for short-term dollar sales options in the currency options market has grown, reflecting a rise in demand to sell dollars by exporters and investors.
The dollar/yen risk reversal, which shows the pricing differential between puts and calls, has turned to the dollar sales options' favour since Monday, options dealers in Tokyo said.

"Buying demand for dollar put options with maturity of up to three-months has exceeded that of dollar calls as cautious views have emerged," said Ichiro Ikeda, director of the foreign exchange department at Credit Suisse First Boston in Tokyo.

Before the meeting of the Group of Seven (G7) nations early this month, where G7 monetary officials signalled that the dollar had risen enough, the options market favoured dollar call options even in the longer-term options.
